title: Spanner, CockroachDB & DynamoDB
description: Go deep into how three production distributed databases solve the hardest problems in distributed systems.

segments.text: We're going to dissect three production distributed databases: Google Spanner, CockroachDB, and Amazon DynamoDB. Each made radically different design choices. Understanding why teaches you more than any textbook.

Spanner chose strong consistency with global scale. CockroachDB brought Spanner's ideas to open source without GPS clocks. DynamoDB chose availability and partition tolerance, sacrificing strong consistency. Different trade-offs, different use cases.

Spanner's secret weapon is TrueTime — an API backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every Google datacenter. It returns a time interval with guaranteed bounds. You know the real time is somewhere within that interval. No other company has this.
segments.thought_prompt: Why can't Spanner just use NTP like everyone else?

segments.text: Spanner uses TrueTime to assign globally ordered timestamps to transactions. It waits out the uncertainty interval before committing — guaranteeing external consistency. This means if transaction A finishes before B starts, A's timestamp is always less than B's.

CockroachDB can't use GPS clocks — it runs on commodity hardware. Instead, it uses Raft consensus for every range of data. Each range is a Raft group with a leader that serializes writes. Hybrid-logical clocks handle ordering across ranges.

CockroachDB splits data into 512MB ranges. Each range is replicated via Raft across nodes. When a range gets too large, it splits. When a node goes down, Raft handles failover within seconds. Multi-active — any node can serve reads and writes.

DynamoDB uses consistent hashing to partition data across nodes. Each partition handles a slice of the hash space. When traffic spikes, partitions split automatically. No Raft, no Paxos — DynamoDB optimizes for availability over strong consistency.

DynamoDB uses sloppy quorum for replication. Writes go to W nodes, reads from R nodes. If W plus R exceeds the replication factor, you get strong consistency. By default, DynamoDB uses eventual consistency — faster reads, slightly stale data.
segments.thought_prompt: With replication factor 3, what values of W and R guarantee strong consistency?

segments.text: Spanner: globally consistent, needs special hardware, higher latency due to commit-wait. CockroachDB: serializable without GPS clocks, Raft overhead per range. DynamoDB: fastest writes, eventual consistency by default, single-digit millisecond latency at any scale.

There's no best distributed database. Spanner wins when you need global strong consistency. CockroachDB wins when you want Spanner-like guarantees on commodity hardware. DynamoDB wins when you need massive write throughput with flexible consistency. Know the trade-offs.
